title: Complex numbers I: algebra and geometry

problems.html: Simplify the powers of the imaginary unit i3,i4,i15,i2026,i−1,i−7.\mathrm{i}^{3},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{4},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{15},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{2026},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{-1},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{-7}.i3,i4,i15,i2026,i−1,i−7.
hints: The powers of i\mathrm{i}i cycle with period 444: i0=1\mathrm{i}^0=1i0=1, i1=i\mathrm{i}^1=\mathrm{i}i1=i, i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1, i3=−i\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}i3=−i, and then it begins again.
For a positive exponent, divide by 444 and keep only the remainder — 15=4⋅3+315=4\cdot3+315=4⋅3+3 sends you to i3\mathrm{i}^3i3.

Negative exponents behave the same way once you know i−1=1i=ii2=−i\mathrm{i}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{i}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}^2}=-\mathrm{i}i−1=i1​=i2i​=−i; alternatively add multiples of 444 to the exponent until it turns positive.
problems.format: the six values in order, comma-separated

hints: Addition and subtraction act part by part: real with real, imaginary with imaginary.
Multiplication is ordinary bracket expansion — the one new rule is that i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 becomes −1-1−1.
Watch the sign as the i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 term joins the real part: in zwzwzw the term −10i2-10\mathrm{i}^2−10i2 contributes +10+10+10, not −10-10−10.

problems.html:
Let z=2+3iz=2+3\mathrm{i}z=2+3i and w=1−4iw=1-4\mathrm{i}w=1−4i (as in the notes).

  1. Compute zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in Cartesian form.

  2. Verify the conjugate rule zw‾=z‾ w‾\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}zw=zw.

  3. Verify the modulus rule ∣zw∣=∣z∣ ∣w∣\left|zw\right|=\left|z\right|\,\left|w\right|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣.
hints: Part (a) is one expansion and one division; parts (b) and (c) are checks, so compute each side separately and compare.
For z/wz/wz/w, multiply top and bottom by wˉ=1+4i\bar w=1+4\mathrm{i}wˉ=1+4i; the denominator becomes 12+42=171^2+4^2=1712+42=17.
In (c) do not expand anything: ∣z∣=13|z|=\sqrt{13}∣z∣=13​ and ∣w∣=17|w|=\sqrt{17}∣w∣=17​, so the claim is simply that ∣zw∣=13⋅17|zw|=\sqrt{13\cdot17}∣zw∣=13⋅17​.

problems.html: (Maths stream — a general proof.) Let z=a+b iz=a+b\,\mathrm{i}z=a+bi and w=c+d iw=c+d\,\mathrm{i}w=c+di with a,b,c,d∈Ra,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}a,b,c,d∈R. Prove the conjugate-of-a-product rule zw‾=z‾ w‾\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}zw=zw directly from the definition a+bi‾=a−bi\overline{a+b\mathrm{i}}=a-b\mathrm{i}a+bi​=a−bi.
hints: Everything follows from expanding both sides in terms of a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d; no cleverness is required.
Multiply out zwzwzw first and collect it as (real part) +++ (real part) i\,\mathrm{i}i, then conjugate by flipping the sign of that imaginary part.
Now expand zˉ wˉ=(a−bi)(c−di)\bar z\,\bar w=(a-b\mathrm{i})(c-d\mathrm{i})zˉwˉ=(a−bi)(c−di) independently and compare the two results term by term.

problems.html:
Solve over C\mathbb{C}C, and confirm that the roots form a conjugate pair:

  1. x2+2x+10=0x^2+2x+10=0x2+2x+10=0; (b) x2−4x+13=0x^2-4x+13=0x2−4x+13=0; (c) 2x2+x+1=02x^2+x+1=02x2+x+1=0.
hints: The method is unchanged from real quadratics. The only difference is that a negative discriminant is now allowed rather than fatal.
Completing the square is quickest for (a) and (b): (x+1)2+9=0(x+1)^2+9=0(x+1)2+9=0 says (x+1)2=−9(x+1)^2=-9(x+1)2=−9.
For (c) use the quadratic formula and write −7\sqrt{-7}−7​ as i7\mathrm{i}\sqrt7i7​. Check that each pair of roots are conjugates — with real coefficients they must be.
problems.format: roots of (a), (b) with positive Im part

problems.html: Find the real numbers x,yx,yx,y satisfying (x+y i)(3−i)=7+i(x+y\,\mathrm{i})(3-\mathrm{i})=7+\mathrm{i}(x+yi)(3−i)=7+i.
hints: Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree — that turns one complex equation into two real ones.
Expand (x+yi)(3−i)(x+y\mathrm{i})(3-\mathrm{i})(x+yi)(3−i) and collect it into that shape; you should reach (3x+y)+(3y−x)i(3x+y)+(3y-x)\mathrm{i}(3x+y)+(3y−x)i.
Now solve the simultaneous pair 3x+y=73x+y=73x+y=7 and 3y−x=13y-x=13y−x=1, then substitute back into the original product as a check.

problems.html: Let z=3+2iz=3+2\mathrm{i}z=3+2i and w=−1+2iw=-1+2\mathrm{i}w=−1+2i. Plot z, w, z‾, z+w, z−wz,\ w,\ \overline{z},\ z+w,\ z-wz, w, z, z+w, z−w on an Argand diagram, and compute the distance ∣z−w∣\left|z-w\right|∣z−w∣ between the points zzz and www.
hints: Plot each number as a point (a,b)(a,b)(a,b); the conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis.
Notice that z−wz-wz−w comes out purely real here — the two points share the same imaginary part, so the difference is horizontal.
∣z−w∣|z-w|∣z−w∣ is the distance between the two points. That reading of the modulus is the one to remember from this unit.

problems.html:
(Physics — AC circuits.) A series circuit has complex impedance Z=4+3iZ=4+3\mathrm{i}Z=4+3i (in ohms). It is driven by a voltage V=10V=10V=10 (volts, taken as a real reference).

  1. Find ∣Z∣\left|Z\right|∣Z∣ and the phase angle ArgZ\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}ZArgZ.

  2. Compute the current I=V/ZI=V/ZI=V/Z in Cartesian form and its magnitude ∣I∣\left|I\right|∣I∣.
hints: The modulus and phase angle of ZZZ are just its polar form; sketch 4+3i4+3\mathrm{i}4+3i to confirm the quadrant before trusting an arctangent.
4+3i4+3\mathrm{i}4+3i is a 333–444–555 triangle, so the modulus is a whole number. It lies in the first quadrant, so arctan⁡(3/4)\arctan(3/4)arctan(3/4) is the correct principal argument here.
For the current, divide by multiplying top and bottom by Zˉ=4−3i\bar Z=4-3\mathrm{i}Zˉ=4−3i. Then check with ∣I∣=∣V∣/∣Z∣|I|=|V|/|Z|∣I∣=∣V∣/∣Z∣, which sidesteps the arithmetic entirely.

problems.html: (Data science — distance between records.) Two data points in the plane are encoded as complex numbers p=2+5ip=2+5\mathrm{i}p=2+5i and q=6+2iq=6+2\mathrm{i}q=6+2i. Compute the Euclidean distance ∣p−q∣\left|p-q\right|∣p−q∣ between them and the midpoint 12(p+q)\tfrac12(p+q)21​(p+q).
hints: A complex number is a point in the plane, so ∣p−q∣|p-q|∣p−q∣ is exactly the Euclidean distance between the two records.
Subtract part by part first, and only then take the modulus of the result.
The midpoint is the ordinary average 12(p+q)\tfrac12(p+q)21​(p+q) — average the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

problems.html: Convert each number to polar form, giving the principal argument Argz∈(−π,π]\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}z\in(-\pi,\pi]Argz∈(−π,π]. Sketch each to fix the quadrant. (a) −1+i;(b) −2−23 i;(c) 3−i;(d) −5.\text{(a)}\ -1+\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ -2-2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \sqrt3-\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ -5.(a) −1+i;(b) −2−23​i;(c) 3​−i;(d) −5.

problems.html: Let z=2(cos⁡3π4+isin⁡3π4)z=\sqrt2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{3\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\bigr)z=2​(cos43π​+isin43π​) and w=2(cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2)w=2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\bigr)w=2(cos2π​+isin2π​). problems.html:
1. For z=2+iz=2+\mathrm{i}z=2+i, compute iz\mathrm{i}ziz and confirm geometrically that multiplying by i\mathrm{i}i is a quarter-turn anticlockwise that preserves length.

  2. Which single complex number rotates a point by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ anticlockwise and doubles its distance from the origin?

  3. Apply a clockwise quarter-turn to 3+i3+\mathrm{i}3+i (i.e. multiply by the number of modulus 111 and argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​).
hints: Multiplying by a number of modulus 111 rotates without changing length, and multiplying by i\mathrm{i}i is the quarter-turn anticlockwise.
Test that claim in (a) by computing ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ and ∣iz∣|\mathrm{i}z|∣iz∣ and comparing the two arguments.
For (b) you need a rotation and a stretch at once, so take modulus 222 with argument π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​. For (c) the multiplier of modulus 111 and argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​ is −i-\mathrm{i}−i.

problems.html: Compute (1+i)2(1+\mathrm{i})^2(1+i)2 and (1+i)4(1+\mathrm{i})^4(1+i)4 by direct multiplication, and hence find ∣(1+i)10∣\left|(1+\mathrm{i})^{10}\right|​(1+i)10​ without expanding.

For the last part do not expand anything: the rule ∣zn∣=∣z∣n|z^n|=|z|^n∣zn∣=∣z∣n does the whole job.
∣1+i∣=2|1+\mathrm{i}|=\sqrt2∣1+i∣=2​, so what you need is (2)10=25(\sqrt2)^{10}=2^{5}(2​)10=25.

problems.html:
(Conceptual — true or false, with a one-line reason.)

  1. For every z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C, z2≥0z^2\ge0z2≥0.

  2. ∣z∣=∣z‾∣\left|z\right|=\left|\overline{z}\right|∣z∣=∣z∣ for all zzz.

  3. If z+z‾=0z+\overline{z}=0z+z=0 then zzz is purely imaginary or zero.

  4. Re(zw)=Re(z) Re(w)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(zw)=\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(z)\,\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(w)Re(zw)=Re(z)Re(w) for all z,wz,wz,w.

  5. There is an ordering <<< on C\mathbb{C}C compatible with its arithmetic — that is, one respecting +++ and ×\times× (if x>0x>0x>0 and y>0y>0y>0 then x+y>0x+y>0x+y>0 and xy>0xy>0xy>0), so that every nonzero square is positive.
hints: Each is settled by a one-line reason or a single counterexample. Try z=iz=\mathrm{i}z=i first — it breaks several plausible-looking claims.
For (a), ask whether '≥0\ge 0≥0' even means anything for a number that is not real. For (c), what is z+zˉz+\bar zz+zˉ in terms of Re⁡z\operatorname{Re}zRez?
For (e), suppose such an ordering existed. Every non-zero square would have to be positive; apply that to 1=121=1^21=12 and to −1=i2-1=\mathrm{i}^2−1=i2 and see what you are forced to conclude.

problems.html: (Spot the error.) A student writes the following two lines. Find and correct each mistake. (i)  2+3i1+i=21+31i=2+3i;(ii)  −4 −9=(−4)(−9)=36=6.\text{(i)}\ \ \frac{2+3\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}=\frac{2}{1}+\frac{3}{1}\mathrm{i}=2+3\mathrm{i}; \qquad\allowbreak \qquad\allowbreak \text{(ii)}\ \ \sqrt{-4}\,\sqrt{-9}=\sqrt{(-4)(-9)}=\sqrt{36}=6.(i)  1+i2+3i​=12​+13​i=2+3i;(ii)  −4​−9​=(−4)(−9)​=36​=6.
hints: Both lines apply a rule outside the conditions that make it true. Name the rule before naming the mistake.
In (i), division of complex numbers is never done part by part; the repair is to multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
In (ii), xy=xy\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{xy}x​y​=xy​ needs x,y≥0x,y\ge 0x,y≥0. Convert each root to a multiple of i\mathrm{i}i first, then multiply, and watch what happens to the sign.

problems.html: Evaluate the geometric-looking sum ∑k=02026i k=1+i+i2+⋯+i2026\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{2026}\mathrm{i}^{\,k} =1+\mathrm{i}+\mathrm{i}^2+\dots+\mathrm{i}^{2026}k=0∑2026​ik=1+i+i2+⋯+i2026.

Any four consecutive powers sum to 1+i−1−i=01+\mathrm{i}-1-\mathrm{i}=01+i−1−i=0, so only the leftover terms at the end can survive.
Count carefully — kkk runs from 000 to 202620262026, so there are 202720272027 terms, and 2027=4⋅506+32027=4\cdot506+32027=4⋅506+3. Add just the three that are left over.

Multiply the two known factors together — (x−(1+2i))(x−(1−2i))\bigl(x-(1+2\mathrm{i})\bigr)\bigl(x-(1-2\mathrm{i})\bigr)(x−(1+2i))(x−(1−2i)) comes out with real coefficients — then divide the cubic by that quadratic.

problems.html: Without converting to Cartesian form, evaluate ∣(3+4i)(5−12i)1+i∣\displaystyle\left|\frac{(3+4\mathrm{i})(5-12\mathrm{i})}{1+\mathrm{i}}\right|​1+i(3+4i)(5−12i)​​.
hints: You are asked only for the modulus, so use ∣zw∣=∣z∣ ∣w∣|zw|=|z|\,|w|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣ and ∣z/w∣=∣z∣/∣w∣|z/w|=|z|/|w|∣z/w∣=∣z∣/∣w∣ and never expand anything.
Each factor is a familiar triangle: ∣3+4i∣=5|3+4\mathrm{i}|=5∣3+4i∣=5 and ∣5−12i∣=13|5-12\mathrm{i}|=13∣5−12i∣=13.
That leaves 5⋅132\dfrac{5\cdot13}{\sqrt2}2​5⋅13​; rationalise the denominator if you want the tidier exact form.

problems.html: Describe geometrically (and sketch) the set of points z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C satisfying (a) ∣z∣=2;(b) ∣z−1∣=3;(c) ∣z−i∣=∣z+i∣.\text{(a)}\ \left|z\right|=2;\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \left|z-1\right|=3;\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \left|z-\mathrm{i}\right|=\left|z+\mathrm{i}\right|.(a) ∣z∣=2;(b) ∣z−1∣=3;(c) ∣z−i∣=∣z+i∣.
hints: Read every modulus as a distance: ∣z−c∣|z-c|∣z−c∣ is the distance from the point zzz to the point ccc.
So (a) and (b) each say 'stay at a fixed distance from a fixed point', which is a circle — read the centre and the radius straight off.

In (c) the condition is 'equally far from i\mathrm{i}i and from −i-\mathrm{i}−i', which is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Confirm it algebraically by putting z=x+yiz=x+y\mathrm{i}z=x+yi.

problems.html: Sketch each region in the Argand plane (shade it, and show clearly whether the boundary is included): (a) { z:∣z−1∣<2 };(b) { z:1≤∣z∣≤2 };(c) { z:Rez≥0, Imz≥0 }.\text{(a)}\ \left\{\,z:\left|z-1\right|<2\,\right\};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \left\{\,z:1\le\left|z\right|\le 2\,\right\};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \left\{\,z:\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}z\ge 0,\ \mathop{\mathrm{Im}}z\ge 0\,\right\}.(a) {z:∣z−1∣<2};(b) {z:1≤∣z∣≤2};(c) {z:Rez≥0, Imz≥0}.
hints: Each region is the inequality version of a distance condition, so draw the boundary curve first and then decide which side satisfies it.
A strict inequality leaves the boundary out, so draw it dashed; a ≤\le≤ or ≥\ge≥ includes it, so draw it solid.
In (b) two conditions hold at once and the region between the circles is a ring; in (c) rewrite both conditions in terms of xxx and yyy and the region names itself.

problems.html: Convert to Cartesian form: (a) 6(cos⁡π6+isin⁡π6);(b) 2(cos⁡2π3+isin⁡2π3);(c) 5(cos⁡π+isin⁡π);(d) 2(cos⁡(−π4)+isin⁡(−π4)).\begin{gathered} \text{(a)}\ 6\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6}\bigr);\qquad \text{(b)}\ 2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr);\\[2pt] \text{(c)}\ 5(\cos\pi+\mathrm{i}\sin\pi);\qquad \text{(d)}\ \sqrt2\bigl(\cos(-\tfrac{\pi}{4})+\mathrm{i}\sin(-\tfrac{\pi}{4})\bigr). \end{gathered}(a) 6(cos6π​+isin6π​);(b) 2(cos32π​+isin32π​);(c) 5(cosπ+isinπ);(d) 2​(cos(−4π​)+isin(−4π​)).​
hints: This is substitution rather than conversion: put in the cosine and sine values and multiply through by the modulus.
Angles in the second and third quadrants have negative cosine — for instance cos⁡2π3=−12\cos\tfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\tfrac12cos32π​=−21​.
In (d) the angle is negative, so the sine is negative while the cosine is not, and the two surds cancel to leave whole numbers.

problems.html: Let z=4(cos⁡5π6+isin⁡5π6)z=4\bigl(\cos\tfrac{5\pi}{6}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\bigr)z=4(cos65π​+isin65π​) and w=2(cos⁡π3+isin⁡π3)w=2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr)w=2(cos3π​+isin3π​). Find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in Cartesian form.
hints: Both numbers are given in polar form, so stay in polar form until the final step.
For zwzwzw: modulus 4⋅24\cdot24⋅2, argument 5π6+π3\tfrac{5\pi}{6}+\tfrac{\pi}{3}65π​+3π​ — put both angles over 666 before adding.
For z/wz/wz/w: modulus 4/24/24/2, argument 5π6−π3=π2\tfrac{5\pi}{6}-\tfrac{\pi}{3}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}65π​−3π​=2π​, which puts the answer straight onto the imaginary axis.

problems.html: Compute the product (1+i)(3+i)(1+\mathrm{i})(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})(1+i)(3​+i) in two ways — by Cartesian expansion and by the polar rule — and hence write down its modulus and argument.
hints: The point of the exercise is that the two routes must agree, so carry them out independently and only then compare.
For the polar route you need each factor in polar form: 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i has modulus 2\sqrt22​ and argument π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​; find the same two numbers for 3+i\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}3​+i.
The product's modulus is the product of the moduli and its argument the sum of the arguments. Matching the two forms afterwards even hands you the exact cosine and sine of that awkward angle.
problems.format: the argument of the product; π as pi

problems.html: (Data science.) Encode two real 222-vectors as u=3+4iu=3+4\mathrm{i}u=3+4i and v=4+3iv=4+3\mathrm{i}v=4+3i. Show that the dot product of (3,4)(3,4)(3,4) and (4,3)(4,3)(4,3) equals Re(u v‾)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(u\,\overline{v})Re(uv), and find ∣u v‾∣\left|u\,\overline{v}\right|∣uv∣.
hints: Work out uvˉu\bar vuvˉ as a single complex number first, and only then take its real part.
Conjugating vvv is exactly what makes the cross terms cancel in the real part — try it with vvv unconjugated and watch the identity fail.
For the modulus use ∣uvˉ∣=∣u∣ ∣vˉ∣=∣u∣ ∣v∣|u\bar v|=|u|\,|\bar v|=|u|\,|v|∣uvˉ∣=∣u∣∣vˉ∣=∣u∣∣v∣ rather than the components; both moduli are 555.

problems.html: (Physics — phasors / rotating vectors.) Two voltage phasors of the same frequency are V1=6+8iV_1=6+8\mathrm{i}V1​=6+8i and a second phasor V2V_2V2​ of equal amplitude but rotated a quarter-turn (90∘90^\circ90∘) anticlockwise, i.e. V2=iV1V_2=\mathrm{i}V_1V2​=iV1​. Find V2V_2V2​ and the resultant V=V1+V2V=V_1+V_2V=V1​+V2​ in Cartesian form, the resultant amplitude ∣V∣\left|V\right|∣V∣, and show that ∣V∣=2 ∣V1∣\left|V\right|=\sqrt2\,\left|V_1\right|∣V∣=2​∣V1​∣.
hints: Multiplying by i\mathrm{i}i is the quarter-turn anticlockwise, so V2V_2V2​ needs no trigonometry whatsoever.
Add the two phasors part by part to get the resultant, then take its modulus.
The final claim is a right-angled triangle with two equal legs: ∣V∣2=∣V1∣2+∣V2∣2|V|^2=|V_1|^2+|V_2|^2∣V∣2=∣V1​∣2+∣V2​∣2 with ∣V2∣=∣V1∣|V_2|=|V_1|∣V2​∣=∣V1​∣.
problems.format: V₂ and V in Cartesian form

problems.html: Prove the parallelogram law: for all z,w∈Cz,w\in\mathbb{C}z,w∈C, ∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2∣z∣2+2∣w∣2.\left|z+w\right|^2+\left|z-w\right|^2=2\left|z\right|^2+2\left|w\right|^2.∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2∣z∣2+2∣w∣2.
hints: Do not break into xxx and yyy. Use ∣ζ∣2=ζζˉ|\zeta|^2=\zeta\bar\zeta∣ζ∣2=ζζˉ​ throughout and the whole proof is two expansions.
Expand ∣z+w∣2=(z+w)(zˉ+wˉ)|z+w|^2=(z+w)(\bar z+\bar w)∣z+w∣2=(z+w)(zˉ+wˉ) and ∣z−w∣2=(z−w)(zˉ−wˉ)|z-w|^2=(z-w)(\bar z-\bar w)∣z−w∣2=(z−w)(zˉ−wˉ) separately.
Now add the two lines and look at the cross terms zwˉz\bar wzwˉ and zˉw\bar z wzˉw: they appear with opposite signs, which is the whole trick.
problems.format: either side of the law when z = 3, w = 4i

problems.html: Find all z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi (with x,y∈Rx,y\in\mathbb{R}x,y∈R) such that z2=3+4iz^2=3+4\mathrm{i}z2=3+4i, working directly in Cartesian form.
hints: Write z=x+yiz=x+y\mathrm{i}z=x+yi, square it, and match real and imaginary parts against 3+4i3+4\mathrm{i}3+4i.
That gives the pair x2−y2=3x^2-y^2=3x2−y2=3 and 2xy=42xy=42xy=4; use the second to eliminate yyy.

Substituting y=2/xy=2/xy=2/x produces x4−3x2−4=0x^4-3x^2-4=0x4−3x2−4=0, a quadratic in x2x^2x2. Only the non-negative root of that is usable, since xxx is real — and then xy=2>0xy=2>0xy=2>0 fixes the sign of yyy.
problems.format: both roots; positive real part first

problems.html: Find all complex zzz satisfying z+2z‾=6−3iz+2\overline{z}=6-3\mathrm{i}z+2z=6−3i.
hints: An equation involving both zzz and zˉ\bar zzˉ cannot be rearranged in zzz alone. Write z=x+yiz=x+y\mathrm{i}z=x+yi and let the two parts separate.
Expand z+2zˉ=(x+yi)+2(x−yi)z+2\bar z=(x+y\mathrm{i})+2(x-y\mathrm{i})z+2zˉ=(x+yi)+2(x−yi) and collect the real and imaginary parts.
You should reach 3x−yi3x-y\mathrm{i}3x−yi; now match that against 6−3i6-3\mathrm{i}6−3i and read off xxx and yyy.

problems.html: (Rotation/geometry.) Two vertices of an equilateral triangle lie at 000 and 222 on the real axis. Use multiplication by a complex number of modulus 111 to find the two possible positions of the third vertex.
hints: The third vertex comes from a known side by rotating it about a vertex, and a rotation is multiplication by a number of modulus 111.
Rotating the number 222 about the origin through π3\tfrac{\pi}{3}3π​ means multiplying it by cos⁡π3+isin⁡π3\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}cos3π​+isin3π​.
Both signs of the angle give a genuine triangle, one above the real axis and one below. Check each candidate is at distance 222 from both 000 and 222.
problems.format: the third vertex's real part, then its modulus

problems.html: (Spot the error.) A student claims “∣3+4i∣=3+4=7\left|3+4\mathrm{i}\right|=3+4=7∣3+4i∣=3+4=7” and “Arg(−1−i)=arctan⁡(1)=π4\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}(-1-\mathrm{i})=\arctan(1)=\tfrac{\pi}{4}Arg(−1−i)=arctan(1)=4π​”. Correct both.
hints: The modulus is a length, not a sum of the parts; and the argument is an angle, so it needs a quadrant before it means anything.
For the first claim, apply Pythagoras to the real and imaginary parts — the 333–444–555 triangle once again.
For the second, −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i lies in the third quadrant, so although tan⁡θ=1\tan\theta=1tanθ=1 is correct, the principal value cannot be the first-quadrant angle.
problems.format: corrected modulus, then argument; π as pi

problems.html: Suppose ∣z∣=2\left|z\right|=2∣z∣=2, Argz=π3\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}z=\tfrac{\pi}{3}Argz=3π​, ∣w∣=3\left|w\right|=3∣w∣=3, Argw=π4\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}w=\tfrac{\pi}{4}Argw=4π​. Find the modulus and argument of zwzwzw, z/wz/wz/w, z2z^2z2 and z‾\overline{z}z; convert zzz and z2z^2z2 to Cartesian form.
hints: Nothing here needs Cartesian form until the very last part — work with moduli and arguments throughout.
Multiply moduli and add arguments; divide moduli and subtract arguments; and for z2z^2z2 square the modulus while doubling the argument.
Conjugating leaves the modulus alone and negates the argument. Convert zzz and z2z^2z2 at the end, then check by squaring your Cartesian zzz directly.
problems.format: the moduli of zw, z/w, z², z̄

questions.stem: Why is i\mathrm{i}i defined by the property i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1 rather than by writing i=−1\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}i=−1​?
options: Because i\mathrm{i}i is not a square root of anything.
The two are equivalent; i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1 is simply shorter to write.
Because manipulating −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ with the usual surd rule leads to 1=−11=-11=−1.
Because −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ would have to be a real number.
questions.hint: Apply the surd rule xy=xy\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{xy}x​y​=xy​ to (−1)(−1)\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}(−1)(−1)​ and see what it ends up claiming.
questions.why: The rule xy=xy\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{xy}x​y​=xy​ holds only for non-negative reals. Applied blindly it gives 1=1=(−1)(−1)=−1 −1=i⋅i=−11=\sqrt{1}=\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}=\sqrt{-1}\,\sqrt{-1}=\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=-11=1​=(−1)(−1)​=−1​−1​=i⋅i=−1, which is a genuine contradiction rather than a curiosity. Defining i\mathrm{i}i by the property it must satisfy means the symbol −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ never has to be manipulated at all. There is a second, quieter reason too: −1-1−1 has two square roots, ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i, and no principled way to call one of them 'the' square root.

questions.stem: A student simplifies 2+3i1+i\dfrac{2+3\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}1+i2+3i​ to 21+31i=2+3i\dfrac21+\dfrac31\mathrm{i}=2+3\mathrm{i}12​+13​i=2+3i. What has gone wrong?
options: The moduli should have been divided instead of the parts.
Nothing, as long as the denominator is non-zero.
The sign of the imaginary part was dropped; the answer is 2−3i2-3\mathrm{i}2−3i.
Division is not done part by part; multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
questions.hint: Test the student's rule on a case you can check independently: does 1+i1+i\dfrac{1+\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}1+i1+i​ come out as 111 that way?
questions.why: In general a+bic+di≠ac+bdi\dfrac{a+b\mathrm{i}}{c+d\mathrm{i}}\neq\dfrac{a}{c}+\dfrac{b}{d}\mathrm{i}c+dia+bi​=ca​+db​i — addition and subtraction split part by part, but division does not. Multiplying top and bottom by 1−i1-\mathrm{i}1−i makes the denominator real: (2+3i)(1−i)12+12=5+i2=52+12i\dfrac{(2+3\mathrm{i})(1-\mathrm{i})}{1^2+1^2}=\dfrac{5+\mathrm{i}}{2}=\tfrac52+\tfrac12\mathrm{i}12+12(2+3i)(1−i)​=25+i​=25​+21​i, which is nothing like 2+3i2+3\mathrm{i}2+3i. Dividing moduli is a real rule, but it belongs to polar form and gives only the modulus of the answer, not the answer.

questions.stem: Both 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i and −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i satisfy tan⁡θ=1\tan\theta=1tanθ=1. What is the principal argument of −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i?
options: −3π4-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}−43π​.
π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​, since arctan⁡1=π4\arctan 1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}arctan1=4π​.
5π4\tfrac{5\pi}{4}45π​.
It has no argument, because both of its parts are negative.
questions.hint: Sketch the point first. Which quadrant is it in, and which interval must a *principal* argument lie in?
questions.why: arctan⁡\arctanarctan returns a value in (−π2,π2)\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)(−2π​,2π​) and so can never see which quadrant the point is in — that is why sketching first is not optional. Here −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i is in the third quadrant, so its argument is π4+π=5π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\pi=\tfrac{5\pi}{4}4π​+π=45π​. That is a perfectly correct argument, but the principal one is required to lie in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π], so subtract 2π2\pi2π to get −3π4-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}−43π​.

questions.stem: Which single complex number rotates a point a quarter-turn anticlockwise about the origin and doubles its distance from the origin?
options: i2\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}2i​
−2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i
222
2i2\mathrm{i}2i
questions.hint: Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments. Write down the modulus and the argument the answer must have, then find the option with both.
questions.why: Multiplying by www multiplies moduli and adds arguments, so the doubling needs ∣w∣=2|w|=2∣w∣=2 and the anticlockwise quarter-turn needs arg⁡w=π2\arg w=\tfrac{\pi}{2}argw=2π​. That number is 2(cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2)=2i2\left(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=2\mathrm{i}2(cos2π​+isin2π​)=2i. Each wrong option gets exactly one half right: 222 has argument 000, so it scales without turning; −2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i has argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​, a clockwise quarter-turn; and i2\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}2i​ turns the right way but halves the distance instead of doubling it.

questions.stem: A student writes ∣3+4i∣=3+4=7|3+4\mathrm{i}|=3+4=7∣3+4i∣=3+4=7. What is the modulus, and why?
options: 555, by Pythagoras on the real and imaginary parts.
777 — the modulus is the sum of the two parts.
252525, since ∣z∣2=zzˉ|z|^2=z\bar z∣z∣2=zzˉ.
7\sqrt77​.
questions.hint: The modulus is a distance in the plane, from the origin to (3,4)(3,4)(3,4). Which triangle has legs 333 and 444?
questions.why: The modulus is the distance from the origin to the point (3,4)(3,4)(3,4), so it is 32+42=25=5\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=532+42​=25​=5 — the familiar 333–444–555 triangle. Adding the parts has no geometric meaning and would even give a different answer for 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i, whose distance from the origin is plainly the same. The value 252525 is ∣z∣2=zzˉ|z|^2=z\bar z∣z∣2=zzˉ, which is genuinely useful — it is what makes the conjugate trick work for division — but it is the square of the modulus, not the modulus.

questions.stem: A cubic with real coefficients has 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i among its roots. What follows immediately?
options: −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i is also a root.
Nothing — a cubic may have any three roots.
1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i is also a root, and the third root is real.
All three roots are non-real.
questions.hint: Real coefficients force non-real roots to occur in conjugate pairs. Count how many of the three roots that uses up, and what it leaves.
questions.why: Real coefficients force non-real roots to occur in conjugate pairs, so 1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i is a root as well. That uses up two of the three, and the remaining one must be real, since a third non-real root would need its own conjugate partner and there is no room left. Note that the conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part only: −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i is the negation, not the conjugate, and is not forced to be anything.
